advances: The absolute reflected-mass bound for a nonnegative exponential profile extends to a monotone knapsack with arbitrary finite integer coordinate capacities. Removing all binary coordinates by one heaviest-slice selection pays only the dyadic factor belonging to the removed dimensions. The same node supplies the mixed-integer depth consequence for actual convex bodies whose positive fiber volumes satisfy the explicitly stated support and multiplicative-profile hypotheses.
author: research-agent
external_sources: None. The one-dimensional unrestricted geometric-maximizer estimate and threshold characterization are used from the proof of declared accepted fact `a3507c471fff4ad1`, with the radius and parameter map specified above. The actual-fiber curvature nonnegativity and cutoff depth conclusion are used from declared accepted fact `280b299bc1e87c14`, with unchanged fiber-volume objects and the explicit cutoff alias \(L=\tau\). All other steps are proved here.
proof:
The set \(A\) is finite and contains zero, so \(\widetilde W>0\). We first prove the scalar assertion when every \(L_i\ge2\), then remove this restriction without weakening the dyadic exponent. If \(R=0\), positivity of all \(b_i\) gives \(A=\{0\}\), and \(\widetilde S_0=\widetilde W=1\); thus we may take \(R>0\) in the first part.

We begin with the required finite-geometric estimate. For one integer capacity \(L\ge2\), put \(J:=\lfloor L/2\rfloor\ge1\) and \(Z_L(q):=\sum_{h=0}^Lq^h\), for \(0<q\le1\). We claim that every maximizer \(r\in\{0,\ldots,J\}\) of \((2r+1)q^r\) satisfies

\[
\frac{2(2r+1)q^r}{Z_L(q)}\ge\frac43,
\qquad r(-\log q)\le2.
\tag{1}
\]

The one-coordinate estimate in the proof of accepted fact `a3507c471fff4ad1` is used as follows: its scalar maximizing integer \(m\) is our radius \(r\), its parameter \(q\) is unchanged, and its threshold \(t_m=(2m-1)/(2m+1)\) is our \(t_r\). For \(0<q<1\), that estimate states that every maximizer over all integers \(r\ge0\) satisfies \(2(1-q)(2r+1)q^r\ge4/3\), and, if \(r\ge1\), \(r(-\log q)\le2\). It also establishes that the positive integer \(r\) is an unrestricted maximizer exactly when \(t_r\le q\le t_{r+1}\). At \(q=t_r\), the unrestricted maximizers are \(r-1,r\). These are the only one-dimensional facts imported from that predecessor.

If a finite-range maximizer satisfies \(r<J\), then \(q<1\), since at \(q=1\) the sequence \(2r+1\) increases strictly. The successive ratio \(q(2r+3)/(2r+1)\) decreases strictly with \(r\). Since a maximizing \(r<J\) has its successor available, this ratio at \(r\) is at most one, so all subsequent terms also cannot exceed the term at \(r\). The terms below \(r\) are already covered by finite maximality. Thus \(r\) is an unrestricted maximizer. The imported estimate and \(Z_L(q)\le(1-q)^{-1}\) prove (1), with the second inequality immediate when \(r=0\).

If \(r=J\), comparison with \(J-1\) gives \(q\ge t_J\). At \(q=t_J\), the unrestricted estimate gives both \(2(2J+1)t_J^J/Z_L(t_J)\ge4/3\) and \(J(-\log t_J)\le2\). The latter proves the second inequality in (1) throughout \([t_J,1]\). For the first inequality, put \(x=\log q\) and consider

\[
g(x):=\log\bigl(2(2J+1)\bigr)+Jx
-\log\left(\sum_{h=0}^L e^{hx}\right),
\qquad \log t_J\le x\le0.
\]

The second derivative of the last logarithm is the variance of \(h\) under probabilities proportional to \(e^{hx}\), and is nonnegative. Hence \(g\) is concave, so its minimum over this interval is attained at an endpoint. The lower endpoint was just bounded. At the upper endpoint, the ratio whose logarithm is \(g(0)\) is \(2(2J+1)/(L+1)\). It equals \(2\) when \(L=2J\), and equals \((2J+1)/(J+1)\ge3/2\) when \(L=2J+1\). Both are at least \(4/3\). This proves (1) also for a binding upper radius, including \(q=1\) and every possible tie.

Return to the case \(L_i\ge2\) for all coordinates, and put \(J_i:=\lfloor L_i/2\rfloor\). For \(\lambda\ge0\), define \(q_i(\lambda):=e^{-(a_i+\lambda b_i)}\in(0,1]\), and let \(\rho_i(\lambda)\) be the smallest maximizer of \((2r+1)q_i(\lambda)^r\) over integers \(0\le r\le J_i\). This \(\rho_i\) is the finite-range analogue of the predecessor's unrestricted \(m_i(\lambda)\); the ranges are explicitly different. For a nonnegative integer vector \(j\), define

\[
\sigma_a(j)^2:=\sum_i\frac{a_i^2j_i(j_i+1)}3,
\qquad
\sigma_b(j)^2:=\sum_i\frac{b_i^2j_i(j_i+1)}3,
\qquad
F(j):=b\cdot j+2\sigma_b(j).
\]

These are exactly the variance expressions and resource function \(\sigma_a,\sigma_b,F\) in accepted fact `a3507c471fff4ad1`, with the same coefficients \(a,b\), center \(j\), and tilt \(\lambda\), and no rescaling. In particular, \(F\) is nondecreasing in every coordinate. We will select a finite \(\lambda\ge0\) and a vector \(j\) of finite-range maximizers such that

\[
F(j)\le R,
\qquad
\lambda(R-b\cdot j)\le2\lambda\sigma_b(j)+6.
\tag{2}
\]

All coordinates of \(\rho(0)\) are finite, including when some \(a_i=0\). If \(F(\rho(0))\le R\), choose \(\lambda=0\) and \(j=\rho(0)\); both inequalities in (2) follow. Suppose instead that \(F(\rho(0))>R\). As \(\lambda\) increases, \(q_i(\lambda)\) decreases strictly, and the decreasing successive ratios show that \(\rho_i(\lambda)\) is nonincreasing. Each change occurs at \(q_i(\lambda)=t_k\), for an integer \(1\le k\le J_i\), and decreases the coordinate from \(k\) to \(k-1\). Both values maximize at that event. This describes all changes, including the first change from the constrained endpoint \(J_i\).

There are at most \(\sum_iJ_i\) positive-parameter events. If a threshold occurs at \(\lambda=0\), the smallest-maximizer convention already chooses its lower value, so that event is not a later decrement. Each coordinate is constant on a sufficiently small interval immediately to the right of zero, including when \(q_i(0)=1\). Choose a finite \(\lambda_+>0\) such that \(q_i(\lambda_+)<1/3\) for every \(i\). Then \(\rho(\lambda_+)=0\) and \(F(\rho(\lambda_+))=0\le R\). Order the finitely many events in \((0,\lambda_+]\); at any simultaneous event, perform its coordinate decrements one at a time. Every resulting intermediate vector consists of maximizers at that same value of \(\lambda\).

There is therefore a first decrement that changes \(F\) from above \(R\) to at most \(R\). Let its parameter be \(\lambda>0\), its resulting vector be \(j\), and its preceding vector be \(\widehat j=j+e_i\). Put \(k:=j_i+1\ge1\). We have \(q_i(\lambda)=t_k\), and (1), applied to the maximizing radius \(k\), gives \(\lambda b_i\le a_i+\lambda b_i=-\log t_k\le2/k\). Moreover,

\[
\sigma_b(\widehat j)^2-\sigma_b(j)^2
=\frac{2b_i^2k}{3},
\qquad
F(\widehat j)-F(j)
\le b_i\left(1+2\sqrt{\frac{2k}{3}}\right).
\]

The second inequality follows from \(\sqrt{x+y}-\sqrt{x}\le\sqrt{y}\) for \(x,y\ge0\). Since \(F(j)\le R<F(\widehat j)\),

\[
\lambda(R-F(j))
<\lambda b_i\left(1+2\sqrt{\frac{2k}{3}}\right)
\le\frac2k+4\sqrt{\frac{2}{3k}}
\le2+4\sqrt{\frac23}<6.
\]

Adding \(2\lambda\sigma_b(j)\) proves (2). This finite-event argument does not require rational coefficients \(b_i\) or distinct event times.

Fix this choice of \(j,\lambda\), and write \(q_i:=q_i(\lambda)\), \(\sigma_a:=\sigma_a(j)\), and \(\sigma_b:=\sigma_b(j)\). If \(j_i\ge1\), (1) gives \((a_i+\lambda b_i)j_i\le2\). Nonnegativity of both summands implies \(a_i j_i\le2\) and \(\lambda b_i j_i\le2\). Each nonzero-radius contribution to \(\sigma_a^2\) or \(\lambda^2\sigma_b^2\) is consequently at most \(4(j_i+1)/(3j_i)\le8/3\). Zero-radius coordinates contribute zero. Thus

\[
\sigma_a^2\le\frac{8n}{3},
\qquad
\lambda^2\sigma_b^2\le\frac{8n}{3}.
\tag{3}
\]

Let \(V_i\) be independent and uniform on \(\{-j_i,\ldots,j_i\}\). The variance of \(V_i\) is \(j_i(j_i+1)/3\), so \(a\cdot V\) and \(b\cdot V\) have mean zero and variances \(\sigma_a^2\) and \(\sigma_b^2\). Chebyshev's inequality and a union bound yield \(\mathbb P\{|a\cdot V|\le2\sigma_a,\ |b\cdot V|\le2\sigma_b\}\ge1/2\). If either variance vanishes, its random variable is identically zero, and its event has probability one.

On this event, every coordinate of \(j\pm V\) belongs to \([0,2j_i]\subseteq[0,L_i]\), and \(b\cdot(j\pm V)\le b\cdot j+2\sigma_b\le R\). Thus both endpoints belong to \(A\). Their minimum weight is \(e^{-a\cdot j-|a\cdot V|}\ge e^{-a\cdot j-2\sigma_a}\). The law of \(V\) is uniform on a box of cardinality \(\prod_i(2j_i+1)\), so

\[
\widetilde S_j\ge
\frac12e^{-a\cdot j-2\sigma_a}\prod_i(2j_i+1).
\tag{4}
\]

For \(z\in A\), the tilt gives \(e^{-a\cdot z}=e^{\lambda b\cdot z}\prod_iq_i^{z_i}\le e^{\lambda R}\prod_iq_i^{z_i}\). Summing over \(A\) and extending to the finite coordinate box gives \(\widetilde W\le e^{\lambda R}\prod_iZ_{L_i}(q_i)\). This remains valid when \(\lambda=0\) and some \(q_i=1\). Combining with (1)--(4), we obtain

\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\widetilde S_j}{2^{-n}\widetilde W}
&\ge\frac12 e^{-2\sigma_a-\lambda(R-b\cdot j)}
\prod_i\frac{2(2j_i+1)q_i^{j_i}}{Z_{L_i}(q_i)}\\
&\ge\frac12\exp\left(n\log\frac43-2\sigma_a-2\lambda\sigma_b-6\right)\\
&\ge\frac12\exp\left(n\log\frac43-4\sqrt{\frac{8n}{3}}-6\right).
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}
\]

We have \(\log(4/3)\ge1/4\), for example by integrating \(1/t\ge3/4\) on \([1,4/3]\). Completing the square gives

\[
\frac n4-4\sqrt{\frac{8n}{3}}
=\left(\frac{\sqrt n}{2}-4\sqrt{\frac83}\right)^2-\frac{128}{3}
\ge-\frac{128}{3}.
\]

Since \(\log2\le1\), the logarithm of the last expression in (5) is at least \(-1-6-128/3=-149/3>-50\). The chosen \(j\) is in \(A\), because \(j_i\le J_i\le L_i\) and \(b\cdot j\le F(j)\le R\). This proves the scalar assertion when every capacity is at least two.

We now treat all finite nonnegative capacities. Partition the coordinate indices into \(I_0:=\{i:L_i=0\}\), \(I_1:=\{i:L_i=1\}\), and \(I_2:=\{i:L_i\ge2\}\). Put \(k:=|I_1|\) and \(n':=|I_2|\), so \(k+n'\le n\). Coordinates in \(I_0\) are zero throughout \(A\); discarding them loses no mass. For each assignment \(\xi\in\{0,1\}^{I_1}\), let \(\widetilde W_\xi\) be the total profile mass in the slice with \(z_i=\xi_i\) for every \(i\in I_1\), assigning mass zero to an empty slice. These at most \(2^k\) disjoint slices partition \(A\). Select an assignment \(\xi^\star\) of greatest mass. Then

\[
\widetilde W_{\xi^\star}\ge2^{-k}\widetilde W>0.
\tag{6}
\]

The residual budget \(R':=R-\sum_{i\in I_1}b_i\xi_i^\star\) is nonnegative, since the chosen slice is nonempty and every remaining resource contribution is nonnegative. If \(n'=0\), or if \(R'=0\), this slice consists of one point \(j\): the coordinates in \(I_0\) are zero, those in \(I_1\) are frozen, and those in \(I_2\) must be zero when \(R'=0\). The central summand then gives \(\widetilde S_j\ge\widetilde w_j=\widetilde W_{\xi^\star}\ge2^{-k}\widetilde W\ge e^{-50}2^{-n}\widetilde W\).

Otherwise, work in the \(n'\ge1\) coordinates indexed by \(I_2\), with capacities \((L_i)_{i\in I_2}\), coefficients \((a_i)_{i\in I_2}\), \((b_i)_{i\in I_2}\), and budget \(R'>0\). Their support is \(A':=\{z'\in\mathbb Z^{I_2}:0\le z'_i\le L_i,\ \sum_{i\in I_2}b_i z'_i\le R'\}\). Define \(\widetilde w'_{z'}:=e^{-\sum_{i\in I_2}a_i z'_i}\) on \(A'\), and zero outside; define \(\widetilde W'\) and \(\widetilde S'_{j'}\) by the same sums in these coordinates. This explicitly maps the preceding all-capacities-at-least-two assertion's dimension, coefficients, budget, and center to \(n'\), the restricted coefficients, \(R'\), and \(j'\), respectively. It supplies \(j'\in A'\) with \(\widetilde S'_{j'}\ge e^{-50}2^{-n'}\widetilde W'\).

Lift \(j'\) to \(j\in A\) using the frozen binary coordinates and zero coordinates. Every weight in this slice has the common positive factor \(e^{-\sum_{i\in I_1}a_i\xi_i^\star}\), and hence \(\widetilde W_{\xi^\star}=e^{-\sum_{i\in I_1}a_i\xi_i^\star}\widetilde W'\). Restricting the displacement sum defining \(\widetilde S_j\) to \(v_i=0\) for \(i\notin I_2\) gives exactly that same factor times \(\widetilde S'_{j'}\). Therefore

\[
\begin{aligned}
\widetilde S_j
&\ge e^{-\sum_{i\in I_1}a_i\xi_i^\star}\widetilde S'_{j'}\\
&\ge e^{-50}2^{-n'}\widetilde W_{\xi^\star}
\ge e^{-50}2^{-(n'+k)}\widetilde W
\ge e^{-50}2^{-n}\widetilde W.
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus one global heaviest-slice selection spends precisely the \(2^{-k}\) allowance for the removed binary coordinates, and zero-capacity coordinates spend none. The scalar assertion holds in all cases.

It remains to prove the actual-fiber consequence. All untilded fiber and mixed-volume objects below are those of accepted fact `280b299bc1e87c14`, on the actual body \(C\). The auxiliary scalar profile does not replace those fiber volumes. Choose \(j\in A\) from the proved scalar assertion. Define \(\alpha(v):=\min\{w_{j+v},w_{j-v}\}\), \(\mathcal U_j:=\{v:\alpha(v)>0\}\), and \(\Delta_j(v):=\log(w_j^2/(w_{j+v}w_{j-v}))\) for \(v\in\mathcal U_j\). These are precisely the predecessor's oriented-pair weight, positive-pair support, and curvature; its nonnegativity conclusion gives \(\Delta_j(v)\ge0\).

The support hypothesis makes actual and scalar weights zero outside \(A\). The comparison on \(A\) consequently implies \(\alpha(v)\ge(K/M)\min\{\widetilde w_{j+v},\widetilde w_{j-v}\}\) for every integer displacement, and \(W\le KM\widetilde W\). Thus

\[
\sum_v\alpha(v)
\ge\frac K M\widetilde S_j
\ge\frac{K e^{-50}}M\,2^{-n}\widetilde W
\ge\frac{e^{-50}}{M^2}\,2^{-n}W.
\tag{7}
\]

For every \(v\in\mathcal U_j\), both endpoints belong to \(A\). Applying the same comparison at the center and both endpoints gives

\[
\frac{w_j^2}{w_{j+v}w_{j-v}}
\le
\frac{(KM e^{-a\cdot j})^2}
{(KM^{-1}e^{-a\cdot(j+v)})(KM^{-1}e^{-a\cdot(j-v)})}
=M^4.
\]

Consequently \(0\le\Delta_j(v)\le4\log M\) for every positive pair. With \(\tau:=4\log M\ge0\), let \(B_j^\Delta(\tau):=\sum_{v\in\mathcal U_j:\Delta_j(v)\le\tau}\alpha(v)\), exactly the cutoff sum in accepted fact `280b299bc1e87c14` under the alias \(L=\tau\). We have \(B_j^\Delta(\tau)=\sum_v\alpha(v)\).

The cutoff depth conclusion of that predecessor applies: \(n,d\ge1\), \(C\) is a convex body, and \(w_0\ge K/M>0\) implies \(W>0\). Its maximum over centers and cutoffs is at least the value at this \(j,\tau\). It therefore supplies one point \(p^\star\in S\) such that

\[
h_S(p^\star)
\ge\frac{\ell}{16}\frac{B_j^\Delta(4\log M)}{1+4\log M}
\ge\frac{\ell e^{-50}}{16M^2(1+4\log M)}\,2^{-n}W,
\]

where the last step is (7). The accepted cutoff conclusion selects the point before any ambient halfspace, so the same point satisfies the claimed bound for every closed ambient halfspace containing it. The scale \(K\) cancels, proving the stated consequence.
statement:
Let \(n\ge1\) be an integer, let \(L_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), \(a_i\ge0\), and \(b_i>0\) for \(1\le i\le n\), and let \(R\ge0\). Define \(A:=\{z\in\mathbb Z^n:0\le z_i\le L_i\text{ for all }i,\ b\cdot z\le R\}\). For \(z\in\mathbb Z^n\), let \(\widetilde w_z:=e^{-a\cdot z}\) on \(A\), and let \(\widetilde w_z:=0\) outside \(A\). Put \(\widetilde W:=\sum_z\widetilde w_z\) and \(\widetilde S_j:=\sum_{v\in\mathbb Z^n}\min\{\widetilde w_{j+v},\widetilde w_{j-v}\}\). Then there exists \(j\in A\) such that \(\widetilde S_j\ge e^{-50}2^{-n}\widetilde W\).

There is also the following consequence for actual convex bodies. Let \(d\ge1\), let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^d\) be a convex body, put \(C_z:=\{x:(z,x)\in C\}\), and let \(w_z:=\operatorname{vol}_d(C_z)\), with zero volume for empty or lower-dimensional fibers. Assume that \(\{z\in\mathbb Z^n:w_z>0\}=A\). Suppose that \(K>0\) and \(M\ge1\) satisfy \(KM^{-1}e^{-a\cdot z}\le w_z\le KM e^{-a\cdot z}\) for every \(z\in A\). Put \(W:=\sum_z w_z\), \(S:=C\cap(\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R^d)\), and \(h_S(p):=\inf_{H\ni p}\mathcal H_d(S\cap H)\), where \(H\) ranges over closed ambient halfspaces. With \(\ell:=-\log(1-e^{-1})\), there exists one point \(p^\star\in S\) such that

\[
h_S(p^\star)\ge
\frac{\ell e^{-50}}{16M^2(1+4\log M)}\,2^{-n}W.
\]

For each fixed \(M\), the displayed positive constant is independent of \(n,d,L,a,b,R,K\). This conclusion is restricted to the stated support and profile class. All logarithms are natural.

The scalar tilded quantities use the normalization of accepted fact `a3507c471fff4ad1`, with its support explicitly replaced by the coordinate-truncated set \(A\). The constants \(K,M\) have the same profile-comparison meanings as in that fact. The actual objects \(C_z,w_z,W,S,h_S\) and the constant \(\ell\) have exactly the meanings in accepted fact `280b299bc1e87c14`. The cutoff parameter denoted \(\tau\) below is that fact's cutoff \(L\); it is distinct from the coordinate capacities \(L_i\).
